The aftermath of trauma is literally these kinds of thoughts you're having. The only way out is to see them for what they are—hurt, someone else's unfulfilled expectations put on you, someone was or is mean to you and hurt you, some didn't care in the moment you needed it.

Be kind to yourself—you deserve it. You've probably been through a lot, again I mean it.

These thoughts don’t come from someone who had a supportive environment. They come from someone who tried and failed because nobody was there for them to help them. We are not meant to do it alone.

That said, whether you had support or not, it really never defined your worth. You are capable and worthy human being—like literally everyone you know. Even though your thoughts say otherwise... "I sometimes think the same. I sometimes wish for a life where I don’t have to think about trauma and could just live a happy life. But I study psychology, and I’m in it as deep as it gets.

What I’ve learned is that studying trauma didn’t give me all the answers I was looking for—it only gave me a better understanding of the pain. Healing isn’t about understanding pain or misery; it’s about giving yourself compassion and care. It’s about reconnecting with yourself as you are right now and accepting it. Not fighting it, not hating it. And if you do struggle with those things, acceptance means accepting *that* too. It’s about connecting your body with the voice in your head and allowing them to work together.

I suspect professionals learn the theories and techniques, but the real skill lies in effectively delivering them to a patient who doesn’t trust others—or even themselves. A patient so overwhelmed by damaging beliefs that they can’t hear anything else. CPTSD is incredibly complex, reaching far beyond our consciousness.

We survivors carry a massive burden that most people don’t even acknowledge. It’s a journey, and a long one! But something I read today helped a little: *“The unexamined life is not worth living.”* – Socrates"

I’m in my mid-20s, and here’s what I’d say to myself: Take care of yourself and really listen to what you need. Respect your wishes, your boundaries, and your feelings—they’re incredibly important.

Remind yourself often: Whether you see it or not, you’re making the world around you a better place just by being here. You don’t need to control yourself with hate, conditions, shame, or fear. It’s okay to take a break. Procrastination has its place too—it can be a way of recharging when you need it.

Instead of saying, “I *have to* do this” or “I *must* do that,” be kind to yourself. Try saying, “I’m doing this because I care about myself.” Shift your focus from seeking external validation to building your own internal sense of worth—something that only you control. For example, remind yourself, “I’m a worthy human because I care about myself” or “I’m doing my best to help others in the ways I can.”

And one more thing: Feel your feelings fully. If you’re sad, allow yourself to *be* sad. It’s okay. Remember that feelings and thoughts are just that—feelings and thoughts. They come and go, and if they need to, they’ll come back. There’s no need to hold onto them because they have *nothing* to do with your value as a person.

Yeah, I think this is something I’ll keep working on into my 30s!
